She was referred to the local Same-Day Emergency Care (SDEC) unit for further evaluation.
The following day, the patient re-presented to the emergency department with sudden-onset, severe right upper quadrant abdominal pain.

events.description: Retrospective author hypothesis of rupture mechanism

evidence.quote: Simple hepatic cysts are common benign liver lesions with a reported prevalence ranging from 2.5% to 18% in the general population, occurring more frequently in women and often identified incidentally during imaging for unrelated conditions [,]. Although most cysts remain asymptomatic, complications such as infection, haemorrhage, biliary obstruction, or rupture may occur [-]. Spontaneous rupture is exceptionally rare, with only a few cases reported, predominantly in elderly women [,]. The mechanism of rupture remains uncertain but is thought to involve rapid cyst enlargement, elevated intracystic pressure, and wall weakening due to haemorrhage, infection, or ischaemia, occasionally exacerbated by external trauma [-]. In the present case, the absence of haemorrhage or infection suggests that progressive distension and wall thinning were the likely causes.

summary.text: A 79-year-old woman with hypertension, osteoarthritis and several prior operations developed a week of worsening right flank discomfort and abdominal tightness when dressing, associated with nausea, retching, poor appetite, fatigue and dizziness. Oral tramadol gave partial relief. Initial SDEC examination showed significant hepatomegaly and RUQ/central tenderness without peritoneal signs, while she was haemodynamically stable. Initial blood tests included haemoglobin 131 g/L, WBC 9.1 ×10⁹/L, CRP 106 mg/L and eGFR 52 mL/min/1.73 m². She went home with unspecified analgesia and a planned next-day ultrasound; its performance/result and any baseline cyst dimensions are not supplied. The abstract describes a known cyst, whereas the body reports no prior hepatic pathology or cyst imaging; the baseline history remains unresolved.

She returned the following day after sudden severe sharp constant RUQ pain (10/10), bilious vomiting, subjective fever and chills. Measured temperature was 36.9°C, oxygen saturation 96% on room air, GCS 15/15 and blood pressure reportedly normal; she was stable and afebrile, with mild RUQ tenderness and no longer palpable hepatomegaly. Deterioration tests labeled Day 3 showed WBC 13.5, neutrophils 12.5 and lymphocytes 0.5 ×10⁹/L, CRP 70 mg/L and mild hypokalaemia 3.1 mmol/L. CT described a ruptured right hepatic cyst, 8.1×6.8×10 cm, with lateral wall collapse and perihepatic fluid, without radiological bleeding, infection, malignancy or biliary obstruction. Hepatobiliary discussion favored conservative inpatient care: fluids, regular unspecified analgesia, VTE prophylaxis and monitoring; antibiotics and acute surgical/percutaneous interventions were withheld/deferred. Brief diarrhoea had negative stool cultures/C. difficile assays. Four-day repeat contrast CT showed a larger 12.5×9×15.5 cm homogeneous sterile-appearing perihepatic collection without gas, rim enhancement or septations. She became asymptomatic by the first-week end and was discharged with recurrence safety advice and hepatobiliary follow-up.

At a later unspecified date she underwent elective laparoscopic deroofing for definitive treatment. The operative report locates the cyst in liver segment IV, with its lateral wall adjoining medial gallbladder; this differs from the earlier CT location wording. Hasson access and three ports were followed by extensive adhesiolysis, puncture/aspiration of clear serous contents, harmonic-scalpel deroofing and wall retrieval. Haemostasis involved minimal unspecified blood loss; an omental patch was clipped into the cavity and port sites closed in layers. Recovery was uneventful, oral intake and mobilisation began the same day, LFTs were normal, and discharge occurred 48 hours after surgery. Clinical/imaging follow-up found no symptoms, recurrence or postoperative complications; follow-up date and duration were not reported. Proposed progressive distension/wall thinning as a rupture cause remains an author hypothesis.
